measurementDefinition.name: Measuring the Compression Dividend
measurementDefinition.role: Primary proposed measurement and accounting layer for determining when governed reuse is more advantageous than matched recomputation
measurementDefinition.adaptiveDecisionRule: Recompute when reconstruction is cheaper, the task is novel, or prior state is unreliable. Preserve and reuse when trustworthy prior structure prevents more work than the complete reuse system consumes.
measurementDefinition.dynamicReuseFrontier: The moving workload-dependent boundary where Net Reuse Benefit equals zero and the preferred strategy switches between matched recomputation and governed reuse.
measurementDefinition.economicInterpretation: Falling inference cost does not automatically eliminate the Compression Dividend. It can move the break-even frontier outward, while increasing context size, reuse frequency, agentic recurrence, or reconstruction cost can move it inward.
measurementDefinition.qualityBoundary: Efficiency differences are interpreted only after matched recomputation and governed reuse satisfy the same declared Quality Gate.
measurementDefinition.physicalResourceBoundary: A positive result in tokens, monetary cost, latency, or attributed compute does not automatically establish lower energy, water use, emissions, or lifecycle impact.
measurementDefinition.evidenceBoundary: This page defines proposed measurement concepts and operational accounting structures. It does not by itself establish empirical support, universal applicability, or a positive Compression Dividend for every task, model, or system.

netReuseBenefit.definition: Whether the work actually avoided through valid reuse exceeds the complete cost required to preserve, retrieve, verify, maintain, and repair the reusable state

dynamicReuseFrontier.definition: The moving decision boundary where the measured advantage switches between matched recomputation and governed reuse as recomputation cost, task and context size, reuse frequency, agentic recurrence, retrieval cost, verification burden, state stability, maintenance burden, and repair probability change
dynamicReuseFrontier.interpretation: One side of the boundary favors recomputation; the other favors governed reuse. The boundary is workload-dependent and may move as model economics, context size, recurrence, verification burden, or state stability change.

reuseBreakEvenPoint.definition: The earliest valid reuse event at which cumulative work avoided through reuse offsets the cumulative cost required to create and sustain that reusable state

compressionDividend.definition: The cumulative advantage produced when valid reuse continues to reduce accepted-task work after the complete reuse-system cost is included

knowledgeYieldPerCompute.definition: How productively computational resources create accepted, validated, persistent, reusable, task-relevant knowledge

operationalAccounting.avoidedRecomputationFormula: Avoided Recomputation = Matched Baseline Work - Residual Work Required After Reuse
operationalAccounting.netReuseBenefitFormula: Net Reuse Benefit = Avoided Recomputation - Preservation - Retrieval - Verification - Maintenance - Repair
operationalAccounting.cumulativeDividendFormula: D(k) = Cumulative Avoided Recomputation - Initial Reusable-State Cost - Cumulative Retrieval, Verification, Maintenance, and Repair Cost
operationalAccounting.breakEvenCondition: k* is the earliest valid reuse event for which D(k) >= 0

accountingComponents.matchedBaselineWork: The computational or economic work required to produce an accepted result through matched recomputation.
accountingComponents.residualWorkAfterReuse: Any computation, inference, reasoning, tool use, transformation, or other accepted-task work still required after prior state has been retrieved.
accountingComponents.avoidedRecomputation: The portion of matched baseline work actually prevented by valid reuse after residual work is accounted for.
accountingComponents.preservation: Cost required to create and preserve reusable state.
accountingComponents.retrieval: Cost required to locate and retrieve the reusable state.
accountingComponents.verification: Cost required to determine whether the retrieved state remains acceptable for the current task.
accountingComponents.maintenance: Allocated cost required to maintain, version, index, govern, or otherwise sustain the reusable state.
accountingComponents.repair: Cost arising from invalidation, inconsistency, drift, correction, reconstruction, or other repair needed to restore reliable reuse.

operationalAccounting.interpretationBoundary: Retrieval does not imply zero further computation. Avoided recomputation must be measured against the residual work actually required after reuse.
operationalAccounting.qualityBoundary: Net Reuse Benefit and cumulative Compression Dividend are interpreted only when matched recomputation and governed reuse satisfy the same declared Quality Gate.
operationalAccounting.universalityBoundary: These expressions are proposed operational accounting templates and are not asserted as universal physical laws or universal equations of intelligence.

baseline.name: Matched Recomputation
baseline.description: Reconstruct the required accepted state from the permitted source material without relying on the preserved reusable state being evaluated.

treatment.name: Governed Reuse
treatment.description: Retrieve, verify, apply, and reuse the preserved state while measuring all residual computation and complete reuse-system costs.

matchedEvaluation.qualityGatePurpose: Efficiency, cost, latency, or resource differences count only after both matched conditions satisfy the same declared acceptance requirements.
matchedEvaluation.residualComputationDefinition: Any inference, reasoning, transformation, retrieval interpretation, tool execution, verification, or other work still required after reusable state has been retrieved.
matchedEvaluation.avoidedRecomputationDefinition: The portion of matched baseline work actually prevented by governed reuse after residual computation is subtracted.

adaptiveDecisionRule.recomputeWhen: Matched reconstruction is cheaper, the task is sufficiently novel, prior state is unreliable, verification is too expensive, or reuse overhead exceeds avoided work.
adaptiveDecisionRule.reuseWhen: Trustworthy prior structure prevents more accepted-task work than preservation, retrieval, verification, maintenance, repair, and residual computation consume.

matchedEvaluation.agenticWorkBoundary: For multi-step or multi-agent workloads, total work must include repeated reasoning, retrieval, tool, verification, repair, and reconstruction steps rather than assuming a single isolated inference call.
matchedEvaluation.complexityBoundary: The architecture does not assume one universal computational complexity class for long-context processing. Dense attention, sparse attention, cached computation, restricted attention, linear mechanisms, and other implementations may differ; the benchmark should measure actual cumulative work.
matchedEvaluation.interpretationBoundary: A favorable reuse result is valid only for the tested workload, model, implementation, quality threshold, cost assumptions, and measurement window. It does not establish that reuse is universally preferable.

measurementBoundaries.avoidedRecomputationDefinition: Avoided Recomputation equals Matched Baseline Work minus Residual Work Required After Reuse.
measurementBoundaries.fallingInferenceCostInterpretation: Lower recomputation cost can move the Dynamic Reuse Frontier outward by making recomputation preferable across more workloads, but it does not by itself invalidate the Compression Dividend framework.

expensiveRecomputation.interpretation: When matched reconstruction is costly, governed reuse may recover its preservation and verification investment after relatively few valid reuse events.

commodityRecomputation.interpretation: When reconstruction is inexpensive, small, infrequent, or rapidly changing, recomputation may remain preferable to maintaining reusable state.

highRecurrenceAgenticWork.interpretation: When long contexts, repeated tool chains, multi-step reasoning, or multiple agents repeatedly reconstruct the same reliable state, governed reuse may become increasingly advantageous.

measurementBoundaries.complexityInterpretation: Dense attention, sparse attention, cached computation, restricted attention, linear mechanisms, and other implementations may have different computational behavior. Evaluation should measure actual cumulative work rather than assume one universal complexity class.
measurementBoundaries.multiAgentWorkBoundary: For agentic workloads, measured work should include repeated reasoning, retrieval, tool use, verification, repair, and reconstruction across the evaluated task sequence.
measurementBoundaries.interpretationBoundary: A measured advantage applies only to the tested model, workload, implementation, quality threshold, reuse architecture, cost assumptions, and evaluation window. The framework permits recomputation, governed reuse, break-even, negative, neutral, failed, and inconclusive outcomes.

computationalEconomicLayer.boundary: These measures can establish a bounded computational or economic result for the tested workload, but they do not by themselves establish a physical-resource or environmental result.

physicalResourceExtension.interpretation: Physical-resource claims require separately measured or credibly attributed energy, facility, cooling, water, emissions, rebound, displacement, and lifecycle effects when those quantities are relevant.

environmentalEvidenceBoundary.frontierInterpretation: Crossing the Dynamic Reuse Frontier establishes only that governed reuse became preferable to matched recomputation under the declared computational or economic measurement conditions. It does not establish that the same crossover occurred for electricity, water, emissions, or lifecycle impact.
environmentalEvidenceBoundary.environmentalBreakEvenInterpretation: A workload may cross the computational reuse break-even point without crossing an environmental break-even point, or vice versa, because energy systems, hardware utilization, facility overhead, cooling, emissions intensity, and lifecycle effects may behave differently from token, latency, or monetary-cost measures.
environmentalEvidenceBoundary.interpretationBoundary: Computational efficiency, monetary savings, lower latency, reduced token use, a positive Net Reuse Benefit, or a positive Compression Dividend must not be translated directly into energy, water, emissions, or lifecycle claims without separate physical-resource evidence.

frameworkEvaluationPath.interpretationBoundary: Canonical authority, measurement definition, a measured Dynamic Reuse Frontier, a reuse break-even crossing, a positive Net Reuse Benefit, a positive Compression Dividend, protocol publication, benchmark implementation, schema validity, machine discovery, licensing, x402 payment, settlement, retrieval, and successful delivery do not by themselves establish independent empirical validation, universal applicability, model certification, production certification, or guaranteed performance improvement. Each result remains bounded to the tested model, workload, implementation, Quality Gate, cost assumptions, measurement window, and evidence state.
